# model__prediction__generic__null-model — full documentation

> Complete inlined content of the documentation pages, for LLM context windows.

<doc title="Contributor Guide" path="onboarding/contributor-guide.md">
# Contributor Guide

This guide assumes you can read Python and have used pandas at least once. It
does not assume you know EPISERVE, forecasting, or this repository.

## Prerequisites → new → deferred

| You should already know | This guide introduces | Deliberately deferred |
|---|---|---|
| Python functions, type hints, exceptions | The `/work` container contract | Kubernetes Job internals |
| pandas `Series`/`DataFrame` basics | JSON Schema validation | Prefect orchestration |
| pytest basics | Direct vs recursive forecasting | lakeFS object layout |
| git branches and PRs | The model card as a contract | Benchmark scoring formulas |

## Part I — The domain in one page

A **forecast model** on EPISERVE is a container. It receives a time series and a
JSON config, and returns a table of future values. Nothing else crosses the
boundary. This model's answer is deliberately boring: it computes one number from
the recent past and repeats it
([`src/model.py:1-10`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/model.py#L1-L10)).

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Input
        C["config.json"]
        P["input.parquet"]
    end
    subgraph Container["python src/run.py"]
        V["validate"] --> S["slice window"] --> F["forecast"]
    end
    subgraph Output
        T["predictions.tsv"]
    end
    C --> V
    P --> S
    F --> T

    classDef dark fill:#2d333b,stroke:#6d5dfc,color:#e6edf3
    class C,P,V,S,F,T dark
```

<!-- Sources: src/run.py:47-148 -->

Two ideas make the rest of the codebase legible:

1. **The window is the model.** Everything before `forecast()` exists to turn
   files into two clean `Series`; everything after exists to turn one number into
   a TSV ([`src/run.py:121-145`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/run.py#L121-L145)).
2. **The card is the contract.** User-facing parameter bounds live in
   `fdo.json` and are enforced through `jsonschema`; a few structural constants
   (`MIN_CONTEXT`, `MAX_PREDICTION_STEPS`) are mirrored in the card and checked
   by the tests
   ([`src/config_schema.py:38-72`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/config_schema.py#L38-L72)).

## Part II — The four modules

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class run {
        +main() int
        +_work_dir() Path
        +_fail(msg) int
    }
    class config_schema {
        +load_parameters() dict
        +validate_config(config) tuple
    }
    class series {
        +future_values(x, steps) tuple
        +prepare_target(y) ndarray
    }
    class model {
        +forecast(x, y, H, statistic) DataFrame
    }
    run --> config_schema
    run --> model
    model --> series
```

<!-- Sources: src/run.py:25-26, src/model.py:15, src/series.py, src/config_schema.py -->

| Module | You touch it when… | Read first |
|---|---|---|
| `src/run.py` | changing I/O, error messages, window selection | [`run.py:47-148`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/run.py#L47-L148) |
| `src/config_schema.py` | adding/renaming a parameter, changing validation text | [`config_schema.py:102-134`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/config_schema.py#L102-L134) |
| `src/series.py` | supporting a new axis kind or gap policy | [`series.py:136-257`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/series.py#L136-L257) |
| `src/model.py` | changing the forecast statistic or interval | [`model.py:27-116`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/model.py#L27-L116) |

<!-- Sources: repository layout -->

Start at `run.py` because it is the only place that knows the order of
operations; every other module is called from there.

## Part III — Getting productive

### Setup

```bash
git clone https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model.git
cd model__prediction__generic__null-model
python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt -r requirements-test.txt
pytest tests/ -v
```

You should see 83 passing tests in a few seconds.

### Your first task: change a message

A good first change is improving one error message in `_describe`
([`src/config_schema.py:75-99`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/config_schema.py#L75-L99)).
The loop is:

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant You
    participant Test as tests/test_config_schema.py
    participant Code as src/config_schema.py

    You->>Test: run the failing/expected case
    Test-->>You: red
    You->>Code: change _describe
    You->>Test: pytest
    Test-->>You: green
    You->>You: commit + push + PR
```

<!-- Sources: tests/test_config_schema.py:99-138, src/config_schema.py:75-99 -->

### Adding a parameter (the full checklist)

This is the most common non-trivial change, and it touches five places:

| Step | File | Why |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Declare it | `fdo.json` → `episerve:parameters.properties` | The card is the source of truth |
| 2. Give it a default/bounds | same block | Validation and API prefill |
| 3. Read it | `src/run.py:84-87` | Pass it to the model |
| 4. Implement it | `src/model.py` or `src/series.py` | Behaviour |
| 5. Test it | `tests/test_*.py` | Lock the contract |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["fdo.json"] --> B["config_schema<br>validates"]
    B --> C["run.py<br>resolves"]
    C --> D["model/series<br>uses"]
    D --> E["tests<br>assert"]

    classDef dark fill:#2d333b,stroke:#6d5dfc,color:#e6edf3
    class A,B,C,D,E dark
```

<!-- Sources: fdo.json:31-67, src/run.py:84-87, tests/test_config_schema.py:22-63 -->

`tests/test_config_schema.py:22-63` is the guard that keeps the card and the
Python constants in sync; if you add a bound, add it there too.

### Testing strategy

| Layer | File | Style |
|---|---|---|
| Pure functions | `test_series.py`, `test_model.py` | construct a Series, assert output |
| Card/validator | `test_config_schema.py` | parameterised bad configs |
| CLI end-to-end | `test_run.py` | temp `WORK_DIR`, call `main()`, read TSV |

Run the static checks and one test while iterating:

```bash
ruff check src tests
mypy src
pytest tests/test_model.py::test_quantiles_are_empirical_quantiles_of_the_window -v
```

### Debugging

| Symptom | First check |
|---|---|
| `config.json not found` | `WORK_DIR` and `_work_dir()` |
| `x values must have a uniform step` | print `x.diff().value_counts()` |
| `history must contain at least 3 points` | window slice indices |
| Output columns wrong | input column order (time first, target second) |

## Glossary

| Term | Meaning here |
|---|---|
| **Window** | The `history_length` rows whose statistic is repeated |
| **Offset** | Rows skipped at the end, for back-testing |
| **Direct forecast** | Compute once, repeat; no feedback of predictions |
| **Recursive forecast** | Feed each prediction back into the window (not implemented) |
| **Null model** | A baseline with no trend/seasonality/covariates |
| **Model card** | `fdo.json`, the machine-readable contract |
| **`episerve:parameters`** | The JSON Schema inside the card |

## Contribution workflow

1. Branch from `main`.
2. Make the smallest change that satisfies the card.
3. `ruff check src tests`, `mypy src`, `pytest tests/ -v --cov=src` — all green.
4. `episerve-validate fdo.json` if the card changed.
5. Open a PR; CI runs the card check and the in-image tests.
6. Merge; `main` publishes `:latest` automatically.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Branch
    Branch --> Edit
    Edit --> Test
    Test --> Edit: red
    Test --> PR: green
    PR --> CI
    CI --> Edit: red
    CI --> Merge: green
    Merge --> Publish
    Publish --> [*]
```

<!-- Sources: .github/workflows/publish.yml:17-83 -->

<doc title="Staff Engineer Guide" path="onboarding/staff-engineer-guide.md">
# Staff Engineer Guide

## The one insight

**The model is not the code; the window is the model.** Everything else is a
plumbing decision about how to obtain a clean window and how to serialize one
number. Once you accept that, the absence of a framework, a model registry or a
dependency-injection layer is not an omission — it is the design
([`src/model.py:1-10`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/model.py#L1-L10)).

The corollary is that the risk surface is not in the forecast; it is in the
boundary. Axis inference, gap policy, config validation and the error contract
are where runs fail and where platform compatibility is won or lost
([`src/series.py:136-257`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/series.py#L136-L257)).

## System shape

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph Boundary["Container boundary"]
        direction LR
        IN["config + parquet"] --> RUN["run.main"]
        RUN --> OUT["predictions.tsv"]
    end
    subgraph Core["Pure core"]
        direction LR
        CS["config_schema"] --> MD["model"]
        SR["series"] --> MD
    end
    RUN --> CS
    RUN --> MD
    MD --> SR

    classDef dark fill:#2d333b,stroke:#6d5dfc,color:#e6edf3
    class IN,RUN,OUT,CS,MD,SR dark
```

<!-- Sources: src/run.py:25-26, src/model.py:15 -->

The core is pure: `forecast(x, y, H, statistic)` has no I/O, no globals and no
clock. That is what makes the 83-test suite fast and deterministic
([`src/model.py:49-55`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/model.py#L49-L55)).

## Decision log

| # | Decision | Alternative rejected | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Flat direct forecast | Recursive sliding window | Recursion only damps the last difference; worse at the chosen 34-week window (13,340 vs 8,866) |
| 2 | Empirical q10/q90 | Parametric normal interval | No distributional assumption; honest for skewed windows |
| 3 | Clamp point into interval | Report incoherent interval | A point outside its own interval is unusable for scoring |
| 4 | Card-driven JSON Schema | Python constants + docs | One source of truth for API, CLI and tests |
| 5 | `ERROR:` line, exit 1 | Traceback | Runner must parse failures without Python knowledge |
| 6 | First two columns only | Named target lookup | Works on covariate benchmark inputs without SQL |
| 7 | String axis → row positions | Reject string axes | ISO-week datasets are common; positions are unambiguous |
| 8 | Gap ≤8 interpolate, else reject | Impute everything | Long gaps are not the same series; fabricating them is dishonest |

Sources: [`src/model.py:27-116`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/model.py#L27-L116),
[`src/series.py:22-25`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/series.py#L22-L25),
[`src/config_schema.py:38-72`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/config_schema.py#L38-L72),
[`README.md:164-172`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/README.md#L164-L172).

## Pseudocode (TypeScript)

The Python is short enough to transliterate, which is a useful test of whether
the design is actually simple:

```ts
function forecast(x: Series, y: Series, h: number, stat: Stat): Row[] {
  assert(h > 0 && h <= 512);
  assert(x.length >= 3);
  const w = prepareTarget(y);                 // fill <=8-row gaps, else throw
  const point = stat === "mean"   ? mean(w)
              : stat === "median" ? median(w)
              :                     w[w.length - 1];
  let [q10, q90] = quantile(w, [0.1, 0.9]);
  q10 = Math.min(q10, point);
  q90 = Math.max(q90, point);
  const future = futureValues(x, h);          // calendar offset or step
  return future.map((xv, i) => ({
    [x.name]: xv,
    ...(future.positional ? { x_auto_converted: xv + offset } : {}),
    [y.name]: point,
    [`${y.name}_q10`]: q10,
    [`${y.name}_q90`]: q90,
  }));
}
```

Compare [`src/model.py:89-114`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/model.py#L89-L114).
The only non-obvious line is the clamp; everything else is data shaping.

## Failure modes

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> BadConfig
    BadConfig --> Rejected: schema error
    [*] --> BadAxis
    BadAxis --> Rejected: NaN/duplicate/non-uniform
    [*] --> BadTarget
    BadTarget --> Rejected: non-numeric / long gap
    [*] --> BadWindow
    BadWindow --> Rejected: history+offset > rows
    [*] --> Ok
    Ok --> Written
    Rejected --> [*]: exit 1, ERROR line
    Written --> [*]: exit 0
```

<!-- Sources: src/run.py:65-146, src/series.py:136-257 -->

| Failure | Blast radius | Detection |
|---|---|---|
| Axis drift (DST, month length) | Wrong future x values | `infer_freq` + tests |
| Long interior gap | Fabricated history | length check before interpolation |
| Point outside interval | Incoherent scoring | clamp |
| Unknown config key | Silent default misuse | `additionalProperties: false` |
| Huge horizon | Memory/time blow-up | 512-step cap |
| Parquet schema change | Wrong column roles | first-two-columns rule |

## Performance

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["read parquet<br>O(rows)"] --> B["slice window<br>O(k)"]
    B --> C["mean/quantile<br>O(k log k)"]
    C --> D["write H rows<br>O(H)"]
    D --> E["total ≈ O(rows)"]

    classDef dark fill:#2d333b,stroke:#6d5dfc,color:#e6edf3
    class A,B,C,D,E dark
```

<!-- Sources: src/run.py:104-145, src/model.py:89-114 -->

The dominant cost is reading the parquet file; the forecast itself is
microseconds. The declared 250m CPU / 256Mi / 5s is therefore a pipeline
statement, not a compute statement
([`fdo.json:111-117`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/fdo.json#L111-L117)).
This is why the model is a good canary: if it takes longer than a few seconds,
the problem is the platform, not the model.

## Tradeoffs

| Choice | Gain | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| First two columns only | Works with any benchmark schema | Cannot use named covariates |
| Card as schema | One contract, no drift | Card edits need care |
| No pinned deps | Simple requirements | Reproducibility risk (acknowledged in README) |
| No recursive mode | Simpler; better at the chosen window | Cannot express momentum |
| String → positions | Handles ISO weeks | Output labels are not real dates |

## When to extend

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["new requirement"] --> B{"Changes the null hypothesis?"}
    B -- no --> C["fix plumbing<br>(axis, gaps, errors)"]
    B -- yes --> D{"Can it be a new statistic?"}
    D -- yes --> E["add enum + branch + tests"]
    D -- no --> F["new model repo,<br>not this one"]
    C --> G["patch release"]
    E --> G
    F --> H["new card + image"]

    classDef dark fill:#2d333b,stroke:#6d5dfc,color:#e6edf3
    class A,B,C,D,E,F,G,H dark
```

<!-- Sources: fdo.json:31-67, README.md:164-172 -->

The boundary is deliberate: `statistic` is an enum, not a plugin point. A drift
model or a seasonal-naive model changes the hypothesis and belongs in its own
repository with its own card, not behind a flag here.

<doc title="Executive Guide" path="onboarding/executive-guide.md">
# Executive Guide

## What it is, in one paragraph

The null model is a deliberately simple forecasting baseline. It looks at a
recent window of data, computes one summary number — the average, the median, or
the latest value — and predicts that the future will stay at that level. It also
reports a plausible range around that number. It trains nothing, downloads
nothing, and runs in about five seconds on a quarter of a CPU
([`fdo.json:111-117`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/fdo.json#L111-L117)).

Its value is not accuracy. Its value is **comparability**: it gives every
benchmark a defensible floor, so a leaderboard can say "this model beats doing
nothing" rather than only "this model beats the other model".

## Capability map

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Capabilities
        B["Baseline scoring"]
        C["Pipeline canary"]
        D["Dataset-agnostic runs"]
        E["Probabilistic output"]
    end
    B --> LB["Trustworthy leaderboards"]
    C --> REL["Faster platform incident detection"]
    D --> COV["More datasets benchmarkable"]
    E --> SC["Coverage and interval metrics"]

    classDef dark fill:#2d333b,stroke:#6d5dfc,color:#e6edf3
    class B,C,D,E,LB,REL,COV,SC dark
```

<!-- Sources: fdo.json:18-29, README.md:1-12 -->

| Capability | Business effect |
|---|---|
| Baseline scoring | Leaderboard claims become falsifiable |
| Pipeline canary | Platform regressions surface in minutes, not days |
| Dataset-agnostic | No per-dataset engineering to add a benchmark |
| Probabilistic output | Enables interval score and coverage, not just MAE |

## Cost and scaling

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["per run"] --> B["250m CPU"]
    A --> C["256Mi memory"]
    A --> D["~5 s"]
    A --> E["no GPU, no network"]
    B --> F["~1/8 of a core"]
    C --> G["fits on any node"]
    D --> H["negligible cluster time"]

    classDef dark fill:#2d333b,stroke:#6d5dfc,color:#e6edf3
    class A,B,C,D,E,F,G,H dark
```

<!-- Sources: fdo.json:111-117 -->

The cost model is linear in the number of runs and effectively zero per run.
The dominant cost is orchestration overhead (scheduling a Kubernetes Job), not
compute. At platform scale the model is cheaper than the metadata written about
it.

## Risk assessment

| Risk | Likelihood | Impact | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Baseline mistaken for a real forecaster | Medium | Medium | Card says "performance floor"; docs repeat it |
| Window tuning overfits a benchmark | High | Medium | Publish parameter choices; compare across benchmarks |
| Dependency drift breaks reproducibility | Medium | Low | Pin versions in a future release |
| Long gaps silently imputed | Low | High | Gaps >8 rows are rejected, not filled |
| String axes produce non-date labels | Medium | Low | `x_auto_converted` makes the convention explicit |
| Leaderboard dominated by tuned baselines | Medium | Medium | Report ranks by multiple metrics; document tuning |

Sources: [`fdo.json:119-127`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/fdo.json#L119-L127),
[`src/series.py:22-25`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/series.py#L22-L25),
[`README.md:164-172`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/README.md#L164-L172).

The overfitting risk is real and worth stating plainly: on the AMELAG benchmark,
changing the window from 8 to 34 weeks moved the interval-score rank from last
to ninth. That is a property of the test window, not evidence that a 34-week mean
is universally better. The baseline should be re-evaluated per benchmark, and the
chosen parameters should be recorded with the entry.

## Investment thesis

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    I["Small, one-off engineering effort"] --> A["Credible leaderboards"]
    I --> B["Cheap pipeline canary"]
    I --> C["Reusable across datasets"]
    A --> V["Platform trust"]
    B --> V
    C --> V

    classDef dark fill:#2d333b,stroke:#6d5dfc,color:#e6edf3
    class I,A,B,C,V dark
```

<!-- Sources: README.md:1-12, fdo.json:18-29 -->

The effort is already sunk and the maintenance surface is four small Python
files plus one JSON card. The return is a permanent, auditable floor for every
forecast benchmark and a canary that exercises the full model-runner path. The
alternative — no baseline — makes every leaderboard claim weaker for zero
savings.

## Recommendations

1. **Keep it deployed and registered.** It is the cheapest trust mechanism the
   platform has.
2. **Label it as a baseline in the catalog.** The card already does; make sure
   the UI does too.
3. **Record the chosen window per benchmark entry.** Avoid presenting a tuned
   baseline as a neutral default.
4. **Pin dependencies before the next release.** The only acknowledged
   reproducibility gap.
5. **Do not extend it into a real forecaster.** New hypotheses belong in new
   model repositories; this one should stay a floor.

<doc title="Product Manager Guide" path="onboarding/product-manager-guide.md">
# Product Manager Guide

## What users get

The null model answers a simple question: **"If we assumed nothing changes, what
would the forecast look like?"** It looks at the recent history of a dataset,
picks one representative number — the average, the middle value, or the latest
value — and predicts that the future stays there. It also gives a range that
reflects how much the recent history moved around
([`README.md:14-26`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/README.md#L14-L26)).

That is intentionally unambitious. Its job is to be the **benchmark floor**: the
number every real model must beat before its result means anything.

## Who uses it, and why

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    R["Researcher"] --> Q["Is my model better than<br>doing nothing?"]
    P["Platform engineer"] --> C["Does the pipeline<br>still work end to end?"]
    L["Benchmark owner"] --> F["Is this leaderboard<br>credible?"]
    Q --> M["Null model"]
    C --> M
    F --> M

    classDef dark fill:#2d333b,stroke:#6d5dfc,color:#e6edf3
    class R,P,L,Q,C,F,M dark
```

<!-- Sources: README.md:1-12, fdo.json:119-127 -->

| User | Job to be done | What they get |
|---|---|---|
| Researcher | Compare a new model against a fair floor | A baseline entry on the leaderboard |
| Platform engineer | Verify the model pipeline after a change | A five-second end-to-end run |
| Benchmark owner | Make leaderboard claims defensible | A permanent reference point |
| Data curator | Add a dataset without custom code | A model that runs on any two-column series |

## The user journey

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant U as User
    participant A as API / CLI
    participant P as Platform
    participant B as Benchmark

    U->>A: choose dataset + horizon
    A->>P: start null-model run
    P-->>A: run finished, predictions stored
    U->>B: add run as benchmark entry
    B-->>U: rank, error, coverage, interval score
```

<!-- Sources: README.md:120-127, fdo.json:18-29 -->

The user never edits code. They choose a dataset and a horizon; the platform
fills in the history window and runs the container.

## Capability map

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Null model"] --> B["Point forecast<br>one repeated value"]
    A --> C["Range forecast<br>10th to 90th percentile"]
    A --> D["Any time series<br>dates, numbers or labels"]
    A --> E["Any dataset<br>first two columns used"]
    B --> F["MAE / RMSE"]
    C --> G["Coverage / interval score"]
    D --> H["No per-dataset setup"]
    E --> H

    classDef dark fill:#2d333b,stroke:#6d5dfc,color:#e6edf3
    class A,B,C,D,E,F,G,H dark
```

<!-- Sources: fdo.json:18-29, fdo.json:69-108 -->

| Capability | Available | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Predict a future level | Yes | One number, repeated |
| Give a range | Yes | Based on recent variation |
| Use extra data (weather, mobility) | No | Extra columns are ignored |
| Follow a trend or season | No | That is a different model |
| Run on a new dataset | Yes | Time column first, target second |
| Run without internet | Yes | No downloads, no weights |

## Known limitations

| Limitation | What it means for a user |
|---|---|
| The forecast is flat | It will not follow a rising or falling wave |
| The range is historical spread | It is not a guarantee of future uncertainty |
| One series per run | No multi-region or multi-age-group forecasts in one call |
| Long gaps are rejected | A dataset with more than 8 missing rows in a row cannot run |
| String dates become positions | The output shows row numbers, not new labels |
| Window choice matters | A different history length can change the result a lot |

Sources: [`README.md:164-172`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/README.md#L164-L172),
[`src/series.py:22-25`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/series.py#L22-L25).

The last one deserves emphasis: on one real benchmark, changing the history from
8 to 34 weeks moved the model from last place to ninth place on interval score.
The baseline is sensitive to that choice, so the chosen window should be shown
next to any result.

## Data and privacy

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Does it store data? | No; it reads the input file and writes the output file |
| Does it send data anywhere? | No; network access is disabled |
| Does it train on data? | No; there are no parameters or weights |
| Does it need credentials? | No |
| What does it keep? | Nothing after the run; the platform stores the output |

Source: [`fdo.json:111-117`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/fdo.json#L111-L117),
[`fdo.json:123`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/fdo.json#L123).

## FAQ

**Is this a real forecast?**
It is a real forecast of a deliberately simple hypothesis: "the future looks like
the recent average". It is not expected to be accurate; it is expected to be a
fair floor.

**Why is every predicted value the same?**
Because the model computes one number and repeats it. That is the definition of
this baseline, not a bug ([`README.md:14-26`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/README.md#L14-L26)).

**Can it use weather or mobility data?**
No. It reads only the time column and the target column. A model that uses
covariates is a different model.

**Why does the range look so wide?**
It is the spread of the recent history. A window that contains a big wave
produces a wide range.

**What happens if the data has gaps?**
Short gaps (up to 8 rows) are filled; longer gaps stop the run with a clear
message ([`src/series.py:22-25`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/series.py#L22-L25)).

**How long does a run take?**
About five seconds, with no GPU and no network
([`fdo.json:116`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/fdo.json#L116)).

**Can we change the history length?**
Yes, it is a run parameter. The platform can prefill it from the benchmark, and
the chosen value should be recorded with the result.

<doc title="Overview" path="01-getting-started/overview.md">
# Overview

## Why this model exists

Every forecast benchmark needs a floor. Without one, a leaderboard cannot answer
the first question a reader asks: *is this model actually better than doing
nothing?* The null model is that floor. It assumes the future looks like one
summary statistic of the recent past and nothing else — no trend, no seasonality,
no covariates ([`src/model.py:1-10`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/model.py#L1-L10)).

It has a second job: because it is tiny and deterministic, it is the cheapest
possible end-to-end test of the model-runner pipeline. If a platform change
breaks image pull, config parsing, parquet reading or TSV output, this model
fails first and loudly ([`fdo.json:121`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/fdo.json#L121)).

| Question | Answer | Source |
|---|---|---|
| What does it predict? | One statistic of the trailing window, repeated for every step | [`src/model.py:90`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/model.py#L90) |
| Is the forecast flat? | Yes, by design: point and interval are identical in every row | [`src/model.py:106-114`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/model.py#L106-L114) |
| Does it emit uncertainty? | Yes: empirical q10/q90 of the same window | [`src/model.py:92`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/model.py#L92) |
| Does it train or download? | No: zero parameters, no network | [`fdo.json:111-117`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/fdo.json#L111-L117) |
| What does it cost? | 250m CPU, 256Mi memory, ~5 s | [`fdo.json:112-116`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/fdo.json#L112-L116) |

## Where it sits

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Platform["EPISERVE platform"]
        API["API server"] --> PF["Prefect model-runner"]
        PF --> K8S["Kubernetes Job"]
        K8S --> IMG["null-model image"]
        IMG --> LF["lakeFS model-runs"]
        LF --> CKAN["CKAN catalog"]
        CKAN --> LB["Benchmark leaderboard"]
    end

    classDef dark fill:#2d333b,stroke:#6d5dfc,color:#e6edf3
    class API,PF,K8S,IMG,LF,CKAN,LB dark
```

<!-- Sources: fdo.json:8-16, .github/workflows/publish.yml:15, README.md:120-127 -->

The model itself only knows about `/work/input` and `/work/output`. Everything
else — pulling the input, pushing the predictions, registering the run — is the
runner's job ([`src/run.py:1-12`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/run.py#L1-L12)).

## What "null" means here

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    S["Observed window<br>y[n-k .. n-1]"] --> P["point = mean / median / last"]
    S --> Q["q10, q90 = empirical quantiles"]
    P --> C{"point inside [q10, q90]?"}
    Q --> C
    C -- no --> W["widen interval to include point"]
    C -- yes --> K["keep interval"]
    W --> R["repeat for h = 1..H"]
    K --> R
    R --> O["flat forecast"]

    classDef dark fill:#2d333b,stroke:#6d5dfc,color:#e6edf3
    class S,P,Q,C,W,K,R,O dark
```

<!-- Sources: src/model.py:89-97, src/model.py:106-114 -->

Three consequences follow directly from that definition:

1. **The output is constant.** If the window mean is 14,029.19, every forecast
   row is 14,029.19. Only the time axis advances
   ([`src/model.py:106-114`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/model.py#L106-L114)).
2. **The interval is a spread, not a predictive distribution.** q10/q90 describe
   how variable the window was, not how uncertain the future is
   ([`src/model.py:7-9`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/model.py#L7-L9)).
3. **It is a direct multi-step forecast.** Forecasts are never fed back into the
   window; a recursive (sliding-window) variant is deliberately not implemented
   ([`README.md:164-172`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/README.md#L164-L172)).

## The forecast horizon

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Observed["Observed history (k rows)"]
        direction LR
        H1["y[n-k]"] --> H2["..."] --> H3["y[n-1]"]
    end
    subgraph Horizon["Forecast (H rows)"]
        direction LR
        F1["h=1<br>point"] --> F2["h=2<br>point"] --> F3["..."] --> F4["h=H<br>point"]
    end
    H3 --> F1
```

<!-- Sources: src/model.py:99-114 -->

The history is consumed once; the horizon is generated from it. Nothing in the
horizon feeds back into the history, which is what makes the line flat.

## Choosing the statistic

| Statistic | Forecast level | Best when | Weakness |
|---|---|---|---|
| `mean` | Average of the window | The window is stationary and not spiked | A single old spike drags the level up |
| `median` | Middle value | The window contains outbreaks or outliers | Ignores a genuine level shift |
| `last` | Final observation | Pure persistence is the right null | Ignores everything before the last point |

Source: [`src/model.py:27-46`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/model.py#L27-L46),
[`fdo.json:56-61`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/fdo.json#L56-L61).

On the AMELAG SARS-CoV-2 benchmark, the choice is dramatic: a 34-week `mean`
gives MAE 8,866 and full interval coverage, while a 50-week `median` gives a
similar MAE (8,559) but an interval score four times worse (151,292 vs 37,756).
The point forecast is not the problem: the 50-week window contains an older
spike that pushes q90 to 152,913, so the interval is enormous. The statistic and
the window length are therefore tuned together, not independently.

## Non-goals

- Not a competitor to real forecasters; it should lose to them.
- Not a seasonal-naive or drift model — both would add trend/seasonality
  assumptions that the null hypothesis explicitly rejects.
- Not a recursive one-step-ahead forecaster (see
  [The Null Forecast](https://the-episerve-consortium.github.io/model__prediction__generic__null-model/02-architecture/null-forecast)).
- Not a data-quality gate: it fills short gaps and rejects long ones, but it
  does not validate semantics ([`src/series.py:221-257`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/series.py#L221-L257)).

|---|---|

| [Configuration](https://the-episerve-consortium.github.io/model__prediction__generic__null-model/01-getting-started/configuration) | How `history_length` and `statistic` change the level |
| [The Null Forecast](https://the-episerve-consortium.github.io/model__prediction__generic__null-model/02-architecture/null-forecast) | The arithmetic behind the flat line |

<doc title="Container Contract" path="01-getting-started/container-contract.md">
# Container Contract

## Why a contract instead of an API

The model-runner does not import this code. It starts a Kubernetes Job with a
shared `emptyDir` mounted at `/work`, puts two files in `/work/input`, and reads
one file from `/work/output` after the container exits
([`src/run.py:1-12`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/run.py#L1-L12)).
That boundary is what lets the platform run Python, R or a compiled binary
without changing the runner. The price is that **everything the model needs must
be in those two input files**, and **everything the platform needs must be in
that one output file**.

| Path | Direction | Format | Required |
|---|---|---|---|
| `/work/input/config.json` | in | JSON object | yes |
| `/work/input/input.parquet` | in | Apache Parquet, ≥2 columns | yes, except `--check-config` |
| `/work/output/predictions.tsv` | out | TSV, one row per step | yes on success |

Source: [`src/run.py:61-67`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/run.py#L61-L67),
[`src/run.py:100-104`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/run.py#L100-L104),
[`src/run.py:143-145`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/run.py#L143-L145).

## The run, as a sequence

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant R as model-runner
    participant C as container
    participant FS as /work

    R->>FS: write input/config.json + input.parquet
    R->>C: start image with entrypoint python src/run.py
    C->>FS: read config.json
    C->>C: validate against fdo.json
    alt config invalid
        C-->>R: exit 1 + ERROR lines on stderr
    else config valid
        C->>FS: read input.parquet
        C->>C: slice window, prepare target, forecast
        C->>FS: write output/predictions.tsv
        C-->>R: exit 0
    end
    R->>FS: upload predictions.tsv to lakeFS
```

<!-- Sources: src/run.py:47-148, src/run.py:143-145 -->

## Input details

### `config.json`

A flat JSON object. Unknown keys are **errors**, not warnings, because the card
sets `additionalProperties: false`
([`fdo.json:31-35`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/fdo.json#L31-L35)).
The schema, bounds and defaults are documented in
[Configuration](https://the-episerve-consortium.github.io/model__prediction__generic__null-model/01-getting-started/configuration).

### `input.parquet`

The model reads the file with pandas and uses **the first two columns only**
([`src/run.py:104-111`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/run.py#L104-L111)):

| Position | Role | Accepted types | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | time axis | date, datetime, isoWeek, integer, number, string | unique, increasing, uniform step |
| 1 | target | number, nullable | gaps ≤8 interpolated, longer rejected |
| 2+ | ignored | any | covariates are not used |

The column names are free. The output reuses the input names, so a benchmark
target called `viruslast_normalisiert` produces `viruslast_normalisiert`,
`viruslast_normalisiert_q10`, `viruslast_normalisiert_q90`
([`src/model.py:103-113`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/model.py#L103-L113)).

## Output details

`predictions.tsv` is tab-separated with a header row. For a datetime axis:

```text
datum	viruslast_normalisiert	viruslast_normalisiert_q10	viruslast_normalisiert_q90
2026-08-19	14029.1917	1468.8	39224.8
2026-08-26	14029.1917	1468.8	39224.8
...
```

For a string axis an extra `x_auto_converted` column carries the 1-indexed row
position, because the model cannot invent new labels
([`src/model.py:99-110`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/model.py#L99-L110)).

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["input columns<br>datum, target, cov1"] --> B["window.iloc[:, 0:2]"]
    B --> C["forecast frame"]
    C --> D["datum, target, target_q10, target_q90"]
    C -. string axis .-> E["datum, x_auto_converted, target, q10, q90"]

    classDef dark fill:#2d333b,stroke:#6d5dfc,color:#e6edf3
    class A,B,C,D,E dark
```

<!-- Sources: src/run.py:123-125, src/model.py:99-114 -->

## Exit codes and error format

| Code | Meaning | What the runner sees |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | success, `predictions.tsv` written | run continues |
| 1 | any handled failure | stderr line(s) beginning `ERROR:` |

Every handled failure goes through `_fail`, which prints exactly one
`ERROR: <message>` line and returns 1
([`src/run.py:29-32`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/run.py#L29-L32)).
Config validation may print several lines, one per problem, before returning
([`src/run.py:79-82`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/run.py#L79-L82)).

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> ConfigMissing
    ConfigMissing --> Fail: config.json absent
    [*] --> Parse
    Parse --> Fail: invalid JSON
    Parse --> Validate
    Validate --> Fail: schema errors
    Validate --> CheckConfig: --check-config
    CheckConfig --> [*]: exit 0
    Validate --> ReadData
    ReadData --> Fail: parquet absent / <2 columns
    ReadData --> Window
    Window --> Fail: history_length + offset > rows
    Window --> Forecast
    Forecast --> Fail: ValueError (axis, gap, horizon)
    Forecast --> Write
    Write --> [*]: exit 0
```

<!-- Sources: src/run.py:65-146 -->

The `except Exception` at [`src/run.py:140-141`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/run.py#L140-L141)
converts unexpected library errors into the same `ERROR:` format, so the runner
never has to parse a Python traceback.

## `--check-config` fast path

`python src/run.py --check-config` validates `config.json` against the card and
exits **before reading any data or importing the forecast code**
([`src/run.py:96-98`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/run.py#L96-L98)).
It prints `config.json OK` and returns 0, or the usual `ERROR:` lines and 1.

```bash
docker run --rm -v $(pwd)/work/input:/work/input \
  ghcr.io/the-episerve-consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model:latest \
  --check-config
```

This is the cheapest way for the API server to reject a bad config before
scheduling a Job.

## Work-directory resolution

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["start"] --> B{"WORK_DIR set?"}
    B -- yes --> C["use $WORK_DIR"]
    B -- no --> D{"./work exists?"}
    D -- yes --> E["use ./work"]
    D -- no --> F["use /work"]
    C --> G["input/ + output/"]
    E --> G
    F --> G

    classDef dark fill:#2d333b,stroke:#6d5dfc,color:#e6edf3
    class A,B,C,D,E,F,G dark
```

<!-- Sources: src/run.py:35-44 -->

In the container there is no `./work`, so the fallback is `/work`. Locally,
`WORK_DIR=./work` makes the same code run without root or a mount
([`src/run.py:41-44`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/run.py#L41-L44)).

<doc title="Configuration" path="01-getting-started/configuration.md">
# Configuration

## Why the config is this small

The model has no hyperparameters to tune beyond the ones that define the
forecast question itself: *how much history*, *how far ahead*, *which statistic*.
Everything else is fixed by the null hypothesis. The card declares exactly four
keys, and `config_schema.py` refuses anything else
([`fdo.json:31-67`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/fdo.json#L31-L67)).

| Key | Required | Type | Bounds | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `history_length` | yes | integer | ≥ 3 | — | Rows in the window whose statistic is repeated |
| `prediction_length` | yes | integer | 1–512 | — | Steps to forecast |
| `prediction_offset` | no | integer | ≥ 0 | 0 | Rows skipped at the end (back-testing) |
| `statistic` | no | string | `mean`, `median`, `last` | `mean` | Which window statistic to repeat |

Source: [`fdo.json:35-61`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/fdo.json#L35-L61).

## The window equation

The window is the slice `[len(data) - offset - history_length, len(data) - offset)`
([`src/run.py:121-125`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/run.py#L121-L125)):

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Data["input.parquet rows"]
        direction LR
        H["history window<br>history_length rows"] --> O["offset<br>prediction_offset rows"]
        O --> E["end of file"]
    end
    H --> P["point + q10/q90"]
    P --> F["forecast<br>prediction_length rows"]

    classDef dark fill:#2d333b,stroke:#6d5dfc,color:#e6edf3
    class H,O,E,P,F dark
```

<!-- Sources: src/run.py:113-125, fdo.json:40 -->

Two constraints follow:

1. `history_length + prediction_offset ≤ len(input.parquet)`, otherwise the run
   fails with an `ERROR:` naming both numbers
   ([`src/run.py:113-119`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/run.py#L113-L119)).
2. `history_length ≥ 3`: with fewer points the empirical q10/q90 are not
   meaningful ([`src/series.py:18-20`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/series.py#L18-L20)).

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant U as user / benchmark
    participant A as API server
    participant C as config_schema
    participant R as run.main

    U->>A: config {history_length, prediction_length, ...}
    A->>C: validate_config(config)
    C-->>A: resolved + errors
    alt errors
        A-->>U: 422 with readable messages
    else valid
        A->>R: start Job with resolved config
        R->>R: cross-field check against row count
        R->>R: slice window and forecast
    end
```

<!-- Sources: src/config_schema.py:102-134, src/run.py:74-87, src/run.py:113-119 -->

The two-stage check is deliberate: the per-key schema runs before any data
exists (API server, `--check-config`), and the cross-field rule runs inside the
container where the row count is known
([`fdo.json:63-66`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/fdo.json#L63-L66)).

## Back-testing with `prediction_offset`

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph File["input.parquet"]
        direction LR
        A["history<br>history_length rows"] --> B["offset<br>prediction_offset rows"]
    end
    A --> P["forecast<br>prediction_length rows"]
    B -. "held-out truth" .-> P
```

<!-- Sources: src/run.py:121-125, fdo.json:49-55 -->

With `prediction_offset=8`, the model forecasts the 8 rows it skipped, so the
output can be compared directly with known values.

## `statistic` semantics

| Value | Code path | Result for window `[1089.8 … 128208.3]` |
|---|---|---|
| `mean` | `values.mean()` | 14,029.19 |
| `median` | `np.median(values)` | 2,953.07 |
| `last` | `values[-1]` | 4,267.20 |

Source: [`src/model.py:27-46`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/model.py#L27-L46).
The q10/q90 are **not** affected by `statistic`; they are always the empirical
quantiles of the same window
([`src/model.py:92`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/model.py#L92)).

## Defaults and unknown keys

Optional keys are filled from the card's `default` before the model sees them
([`src/config_schema.py:127-134`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/config_schema.py#L127-L134)).
Unknown keys are rejected together, not one at a time:

```json
{"history_length": 34, "prediction_length": 8, "horizon": 8}
```

```text
ERROR: config.json has unrecognised key(s): 'horizon'
```

Source: [`src/config_schema.py:84-86`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/config_schema.py#L84-L86).

## Error message catalogue

| Condition | Message shape | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Missing key | `config.json missing required key: '<name>'` | [`config_schema.py:81-83`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/config_schema.py#L81-L83) |
| Wrong type | `config.json key '<k>' must be a <type>` | [`config_schema.py:89-91`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/config_schema.py#L89-L91) |
| Below minimum | `config.json key '<k>' must be >= <n>` | [`config_schema.py:92-93`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/config_schema.py#L92-L93) |
| Above maximum | `config.json key '<k>' must be <= <n>` | [`config_schema.py:94-95`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/config_schema.py#L94-L95) |
| Bad enum | `config.json key '<k>' must be one of 'mean', 'median', 'last'` | [`config_schema.py:96-98`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/config_schema.py#L96-L98) |
| Unknown key | `config.json has unrecognised key(s): 'x', 'y'` | [`config_schema.py:84-86`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/config_schema.py#L84-L86) |
| Too little data | `not enough input data: ... has only N rows` | [`run.py:113-119`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/run.py#L113-L119) |

## Worked examples

### Benchmark run (8-week horizon)

```json
{"history_length": 34, "prediction_length": 8, "prediction_offset": 0, "statistic": "mean"}
```

Uses the last 34 rows, writes 8 rows, all with the same point and interval.

### Back-test against known data

```json
{"history_length": 34, "prediction_length": 8, "prediction_offset": 8}
```

Skips the last 8 rows, forecasts them from the preceding 34, so the result can
be compared with the held-out truth
([`fdo.json:49-55`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/fdo.json#L49-L55)).

### Minimum viable config

```json
{"history_length": 3, "prediction_length": 1}
```

`prediction_offset` defaults to 0 and `statistic` to `mean`.

<doc title="Local Development" path="01-getting-started/local-development.md">
# Local Development

## The shortest feedback loop

The container contract is just a directory layout, so the fastest way to run the
model is to point `WORK_DIR` at a local folder
([`src/run.py:35-44`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/run.py#L35-L44)):

```bash
python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt -r requirements-test.txt

mkdir -p work/input work/output
cat > work/input/config.json <<'JSON'
{"history_length": 34, "prediction_length": 8, "statistic": "mean"}
JSON
# copy or generate work/input/input.parquet (first two columns: time, target)

WORK_DIR=./work python src/run.py
column -t -s $'\t' work/output/predictions.tsv
```

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["work/input/config.json"] --> C["python src/run.py"]
    B["work/input/input.parquet"] --> C
    C --> D["work/output/predictions.tsv"]
    E["WORK_DIR=./work"] -.-> C

    classDef dark fill:#2d333b,stroke:#6d5dfc,color:#e6edf3
    class A,B,C,D,E dark
```

<!-- Sources: src/run.py:35-44, src/run.py:61-67, src/run.py:143-145 -->

No `PYTHONPATH` is needed: `run.py` inserts its own directory into `sys.path`
([`src/run.py:22-26`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/run.py#L22-L26)).

## Validate a config without data

```bash
WORK_DIR=./work python src/run.py --check-config
# Config: history_length=34, prediction_length=8, prediction_offset=0, statistic=mean
# config.json OK
```

This path returns before `input.parquet` is touched
([`src/run.py:96-98`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/run.py#L96-L98)),
which makes it safe to run against an empty `work/input`.

## Tests

```bash
ruff check src tests
mypy src
pytest tests/ -v --cov=src --cov-report=term-missing   # 83 tests
pytest tests/test_model.py -v
pytest tests/test_run.py::test_predictions_are_written_with_the_expected_values -v
```

| File | What it locks down | Tests |
|---|---|---|
| `tests/test_config_schema.py` | Card/model agreement, defaults, error text | 27 |
| `tests/test_model.py` | Point statistics, quantiles, clamping, axis output | 19 |
| `tests/test_series.py` | Axis kinds, uniform step, DST, gap policy | 22 |
| `tests/test_run.py` | Full CLI: config, data errors, TSV output | 15 |

Source: [`tests/`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/tree/main/tests).

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph Unit["Unit tests"]
        CS["test_config_schema<br>card + validator"]
        SR["test_series<br>axis + gaps"]
        MD["test_model<br>forecast math"]
    end
    subgraph Integration["Integration tests"]
        RN["test_run<br>subprocess-level CLI"]
    end
    CS --> RN
    SR --> RN
    MD --> RN
    RN --> OUT["predictions.tsv assertions"]

    classDef dark fill:#2d333b,stroke:#6d5dfc,color:#e6edf3
    class CS,SR,MD,RN,OUT dark
```

<!-- Sources: tests/test_config_schema.py, tests/test_series.py, tests/test_model.py, tests/test_run.py -->

A useful pattern in this repo: `test_run.py` invokes `main()` with a temporary
`WORK_DIR` and asserts on the written TSV, so the tests exercise the same code
path as the container
([`tests/test_run.py:153-170`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/tests/test_run.py#L153-L170)).

## Build the image

```bash
docker build -t episerve/generic-null-model:dev .
docker run --rm \
  -v $(pwd)/work/input:/work/input \
  -v $(pwd)/work/output:/work/output \
  episerve/generic-null-model:dev
```

The image is `python:3.11-slim`, installs `requirements.txt`, copies the repo and
sets `ENTRYPOINT ["python", "src/run.py"]`
([`Dockerfile:1-10`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/Dockerfile#L1-L10)).
There is no `CMD`, so extra arguments such as `--check-config` are appended to
the entrypoint.

## CI/CD

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    P["push / PR"] --> MC["job: model-card<br>episerve_specs action"]
    P --> BT["job: build-and-test"]
    BT --> B["build image (load)"]
    B --> T["run pytest inside image"]
    T --> Q{"push event?"}
    Q -- branch main --> L["push :latest"]
    Q -- tag v* --> V["push :vX.Y.Z + :latest"]
    Q -- PR --> S["stop after tests"]

    classDef dark fill:#2d333b,stroke:#6d5dfc,color:#e6edf3
    class P,MC,BT,B,T,Q,L,V,S dark
```

<!-- Sources: .github/workflows/publish.yml:17-83 -->

Two design choices stand out:

1. **The card job is separate.** An invalid `fdo.json` fails a visible check but
   does not block the image, so a documentation fix can ship independently
   ([`.github/workflows/publish.yml:18-24`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/.github/workflows/publish.yml#L18-L24)).
2. **Tests run inside the built image**, not on the runner
   ([`.github/workflows/publish.yml:57-63`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/.github/workflows/publish.yml#L57-L63)).
   That catches missing runtime dependencies that a host `pip install` would
   hide.

Images built by CI carry the source Git commit SHA in the OCI label
`org.opencontainers.image.revision`, including the tested image and both
published tag variants
([`.github/workflows/publish.yml:60`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/.github/workflows/publish.yml#L60)).
The null model has no weights to pin.

| Step | Command | Result |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Checks + tests | `ruff check src tests && mypy src && pytest tests/ -v --cov=src` | 83 passed, coverage ≥ 95% |
| 2. Card | `episerve-validate fdo.json` | 0 errors |
| 3. Image | `docker build -t … .` | local image |
| 4. Publish | `git push origin main` | `:latest` on GHCR |
| 5. Version | `git tag v0.1.0 && git push origin v0.1.0` | `:v0.1.0` + `:latest` |

Source: [`README.md:120-127`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/README.md#L120-L127),
[`.github/workflows/publish.yml:65-83`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/.github/workflows/publish.yml#L65-L83).

## Common failures

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `config.json not found` | `WORK_DIR` points at the wrong directory | check `_work_dir()` output |
| `input.parquet must have at least 2 columns` | covariates-only file | put time first, target second |
| `x values must have a uniform step` | irregular axis | resample before the run |
| `NaN gap longer than 8` | long missing run | fill or shorten the window |
| `history_length + prediction_offset > rows` | window larger than file | lower `history_length` |

Source: [`src/run.py:65-119`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/run.py#L65-L119),
[`src/series.py:136-191`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/series.py#L136-L191).

<doc title="Execution Pipeline" path="02-architecture/execution-pipeline.md">
# Execution Pipeline

## Why the pipeline is one function

`main()` is intentionally a straight line of about 100 statements: parse
arguments, resolve the work directory, read and validate config, read and check
data, slice the window, forecast, write. There is no framework, no plugin
registry and no dependency injection. For a model whose entire job is one
arithmetic operation, indirection would cost more than it saves
([`src/run.py:47-148`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/run.py#L47-L148)).

| Stage | Lines | Failure mode | Exit |
|---|---|---|---|
| Parse args | 53–59 | argparse error | 2 (argparse) |
| Resolve work dir | 61–63 | none | — |
| Read config | 65–72 | missing / invalid JSON | 1 |
| Validate config | 74–82 | schema errors / bad card | 1 |
| Print resolved config | 84–94 | none | — |
| `--check-config` | 96–98 | none | 0 |
| Read parquet | 100–105 | missing file / parse error | 1 |
| Column count | 107–111 | fewer than 2 | 1 |
| Row count | 113–119 | window exceeds file | 1 |
| Slice window | 121–125 | none | — |
| Forecast | 130–141 | `ValueError` / unexpected | 1 |
| Write TSV | 143–147 | I/O error | uncaught |

Source: [`src/run.py:47-148`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/run.py#L47-L148).

## Sequence

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant CLI as argv
    participant M as main()
    participant S as config_schema
    participant P as pandas
    participant F as model.forecast
    participant O as predictions.tsv

    CLI->>M: --check-config?
    M->>M: _work_dir()
    M->>P: read config.json
    M->>S: validate_config(config)
    S-->>M: resolved, errors
    alt errors
        M-->>CLI: ERROR lines, exit 1
    end
    alt --check-config
        M-->>CLI: config.json OK, exit 0
    end
    M->>P: read_parquet(input.parquet)
    P-->>M: DataFrame
    M->>M: check columns and rows
    M->>M: window = data.iloc[start:end]
    M->>F: forecast(x, y, H, statistic, row_offset=start)
    F-->>M: DataFrame
    M->>O: to_csv(sep="\t", index=False)
    M-->>CLI: exit 0
```

<!-- Sources: src/run.py:53-148 -->

## State machine

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> ResolveWork
    ResolveWork --> ReadConfig
    ReadConfig --> Validate: JSON parsed
    ReadConfig --> Fail: missing / invalid JSON
    Validate --> CheckConfig: valid
    Validate --> Fail: errors
    CheckConfig --> [*]: --check-config
    CheckConfig --> ReadData: normal run
    ReadData --> CheckShape
    ReadData --> Fail: parquet missing
    CheckShape --> Window: >=2 columns, enough rows
    CheckShape --> Fail: too few columns / rows
    Window --> Forecast
    Forecast --> Write: ok
    Forecast --> Fail: ValueError / Exception
    Write --> [*]: exit 0
    Fail --> [*]: exit 1
```

<!-- Sources: src/run.py:61-148 -->

## The window slice

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["len(data)"] --> B["end = len - offset"]
    B --> C["start = end - history_length"]
    C --> D["window = data.iloc[start:end]"]
    D --> E["x = window.iloc[:, 0]"]
    D --> F["y = window.iloc[:, 1]"]
    E --> G["future_values(x, H)"]
    F --> H["prepare_target(y)"]
    G --> I["forecast frame"]
    H --> I

    classDef dark fill:#2d333b,stroke:#6d5dfc,color:#e6edf3
    class A,B,C,D,E,F,G,H,I dark
```

<!-- Sources: src/run.py:121-137, src/model.py:89-99 -->

`row_offset=start` is passed only so a string axis can report absolute row
positions; for datetime and numeric axes it is ignored
([`src/run.py:131-137`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/run.py#L131-L137),
[`src/model.py:99-101`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/model.py#L99-L101)).

## Failure handling

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["exception"] --> B{"ValueError?"}
    B -- yes --> C["_fail(str(exc))"]
    B -- no --> D["_fail('model failed: ...')"]
    C --> E["stderr: ERROR: ..."]
    D --> E
    E --> F["exit 1"]
    G["SchemaError"] --> H["_fail('model card ... invalid')"]
    H --> E

    classDef dark fill:#2d333b,stroke:#6d5dfc,color:#e6edf3
    class A,B,C,D,E,F,G,H dark
```

<!-- Sources: src/run.py:69-82, src/run.py:130-141 -->

The broad `except Exception` at the end is a deliberate contract choice: the
runner should receive an `ERROR:` line, not a traceback it cannot parse. The
comment says so explicitly
([`src/run.py:140-141`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/run.py#L140-L141)).

## Class view

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class main {
        +_work_dir() Path
        +_fail(msg) int
    }
    class config_schema {
        +load_parameters(path) dict
        +validate_config(config, parameters) tuple
        -_describe(error) str
    }
    class model {
        +forecast(x, y, H, statistic, row_offset) DataFrame
        -_point_forecast(values, statistic) float
    }
    class series {
        +future_values(x, steps) tuple
        +prepare_target(y) ndarray
        +coerce_datetime_axis(x) Series
    }
    main --> config_schema
    main --> model
    model --> series
```

<!-- Sources: src/run.py:25-26, src/model.py:15, src/config_schema.py:38-134 -->

## Why this order

- **Config before data.** A bad config should fail in milliseconds, before a
  multi-gigabyte parquet file is read.
- **Column count before row count.** The error that explains the *shape* of the
  input is more useful than a window-size error caused by the same file.
- **Cross-field rule after loading.** `history_length + offset ≤ rows` cannot be
  checked without the row count, which is why it lives in `run.py` rather than in
  the JSON Schema ([`fdo.json:63-66`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/fdo.json#L63-L66)).
- **Forecast before output directory creation.** `output/` is only created after
  a successful forecast, so a failed run does not leave an empty directory that
  could be mistaken for success ([`src/run.py:143`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/run.py#L143)).

<doc title="Time Axis and Target Handling" path="02-architecture/series-handling.md">
# Time Axis and Target Handling

## Why this is separate from the forecast

The null forecast itself is one line of arithmetic. Almost all of the code that
can fail lives in the two preparations around it: deciding what the future x
values are, and turning a possibly gappy target column into a clean array
([`src/series.py:1-10`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/series.py#L1-L10)).
Keeping them in their own module means they can be tested exhaustively without
constructing a forecast.

| Function | Responsibility | Source |
|---|---|---|
| `coerce_datetime_axis` | Turn date-like objects/strings into datetimes when unambiguous | [`series.py:71-104`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/series.py#L71-L104) |
| `future_values` | Extrapolate the horizon for the detected axis kind | [`series.py:136-191`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/series.py#L136-L191) |
| `prepare_target` | Validate numeric target and fill/reject gaps | [`series.py:221-257`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/series.py#L221-L257) |
| `_require_ordered` | NaN, uniqueness, monotonicity | [`series.py:30-45`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/series.py#L30-L45) |
| `_require_uniform_step` | Constant spacing (ns tolerance for timedeltas) | [`series.py:48-68`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/series.py#L48-L68) |

## Axis dispatch

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["x_series"] --> B["coerce_datetime_axis"]
    B --> C{"datetime64?"}
    C -- yes --> D["_require_ordered<br>_datetime_step"]
    D --> E["last + step*(i+1)"]
    C -- no --> F{"timedelta64?"}
    F -- yes --> G["_require_ordered<br>uniform step"]
    G --> E
    F -- no --> H{"numeric?"}
    H -- yes --> I["_require_ordered<br>uniform positive step"]
    I --> E
    H -- no --> J{"object/string?"}
    J -- yes --> K["_require_ordered<br>positions base+1.."]
    K --> L["positional = true"]
    J -- no --> M["ValueError"]

    classDef dark fill:#2d333b,stroke:#6d5dfc,color:#e6edf3
    class A,B,C,D,E,F,G,H,I,J,K,L,M dark
```

<!-- Sources: src/series.py:136-191 -->

The branch order matters: a datetime column is also an object column in older
pandas dtypes, so the datetime check must come first. String labels that happen
to parse as dates are converted; strings that do not (ISO weeks such as
`2022-W01`) fall through to the positional branch
([`src/series.py:85-104`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/series.py#L85-L104)).

## Datetime axes and calendar frequencies

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant F as future_values
    participant C as coerce_datetime_axis
    participant I as pd.infer_freq
    participant T as to_offset

    F->>C: x_series
    C-->>F: datetime series
    F->>F: _require_ordered
    F->>I: DatetimeIndex(x)
    alt frequency found
        I-->>F: "D" / "W-MON" / "MS" ...
        F->>T: frequency
        T-->>F: DateOffset
    else no frequency
        F->>F: diff, _require_uniform_step
        F-->>F: first timedelta
    end
    F-->>F: last + step*(i+1)
```

<!-- Sources: src/series.py:107-133, src/series.py:162-166 -->

Using a calendar offset instead of a fixed `timedelta` is what makes daily data
survive DST and monthly data survive month lengths
([`src/series.py:107-129`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/series.py#L107-L129)).
For sub-second irregularity the code compares nanoseconds with `atol=1`, not a
relative tolerance, so one second of drift on a daily series is not silently
accepted ([`src/series.py:59-64`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/series.py#L59-L64)).

| Axis | Step used | Output | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Daily datetime | `pd.infer_freq` → `Day()` | next dates | 2026-08-18 → 2026-08-19 |
| Weekly datetime | `Week(weekday=…)` | next weeks | … |
| Monthly datetime | `MonthBegin()` | next months | 2026-01-01 → 2026-02-01 |
| Uniform timedelta | first diff | last + k·diff | `0 days 06:00:00` |
| Numeric | first diff (must be > 0) | last + k·diff | `1.0, 2.0, …` |
| String | row position | `n+1, n+2, …` + `x_auto_converted` | `2022-W01` → `3` |

Source: [`src/series.py:136-191`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/series.py#L136-L191).

## String axes

A string axis has no arithmetic, so the model continues it as **1-indexed row
positions** and adds an `x_auto_converted` column
([`src/series.py:186-189`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/series.py#L186-L189)):

```text
x, y, y_q10, y_q90
2022-W01, 10, 9, 11
...
```

becomes, for a window of 10 rows and 2 steps:

```text
x, x_auto_converted, y, y_q10, y_q90
11, 11, 10, 9, 11
12, 12, 10, 9, 11
```

The `row_offset` passed from `run.py` makes those positions absolute in the
whole input file, not relative to the window
([`src/model.py:99-101`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/model.py#L99-L101)).

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["window starts at row 100<br>10 string labels"] --> B["future = 11..12"]
    B --> C["+ row_offset 100"]
    C --> D["111, 112"]
    D --> E["x_auto_converted"]

    classDef dark fill:#2d333b,stroke:#6d5dfc,color:#e6edf3
    class A,B,C,D,E dark
```

<!-- Sources: src/series.py:186-189, src/model.py:99-101, src/run.py:131-137 -->

## Target gap policy

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["y_series"] --> B{"numeric?"}
    B -- no --> X["ValueError: must be numeric"]
    B -- yes --> C{"all NaN?"}
    C -- yes --> X2["ValueError: at least one non-NaN"]
    C -- no --> D["_longest_interior_gap"]
    D --> E{"gap > 8?"}
    E -- yes --> X3["ValueError: gap longer than 8"]
    E -- no --> F["fill leading/trailing<br>from nearest value"]
    F --> G["interpolate interior<br>limit=8"]
    G --> H["float array, no NaN"]

    classDef dark fill:#2d333b,stroke:#6d5dfc,color:#e6edf3
    class A,B,C,D,E,F,G,H,X,X2,X3 dark
```

<!-- Sources: src/series.py:221-257 -->

| Gap location | Length | Action |
|---|---|---|
| Interior | ≤ 8 | linear interpolation |
| Interior | > 8 | reject with an error naming the column |
| Leading | any | fill with first observed value |
| Trailing | any | fill with last observed value |
| Entire series | — | reject |

Source: [`src/series.py:22-25`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/series.py#L22-L25),
[`src/series.py:242-257`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/series.py#L242-L257).

The asymmetry is intentional: a leading/trailing gap means "the series starts or
ends later", and the nearest value is the best available statement about the
edge. An interior gap longer than 8 means the window no longer describes the
series, so fabricating it would make the null model dishonest
([`src/series.py:22-25`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/series.py#L22-L25)).

| [The Null Forecast](https://the-episerve-consortium.github.io/model__prediction__generic__null-model/02-architecture/null-forecast) | What happens to the prepared array |

</doc>

<doc title="The Null Forecast" path="02-architecture/null-forecast.md">
# The Null Forecast

## The hypothesis

The null model asserts: *the future is distributed like one summary statistic of
the recent past*. Concretely, for a window `W = y[n-k … n-1]` and horizon `H`:

```text
point_h = statistic(W)          for every h = 1 … H
q10_h   = quantile(W, 0.1)      for every h
q90_h   = quantile(W, 0.9)      for every h
```

There is no `h` on the right-hand side. That is the whole model
([`src/model.py:49-114`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/model.py#L49-L114)).

| Quantity | Formula | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Point | `mean(W)` / `median(W)` / `W[-1]` | [`model.py:27-46`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/model.py#L27-L46) |
| Interval | `np.quantile(W, [0.1, 0.9])` | [`model.py:92`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/model.py#L92) |
| Clamp | `q10 = min(q10, point)`, `q90 = max(q90, point)` | [`model.py:96-97`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/model.py#L96-L97) |
| Repetition | one row per `h`, same values | [`model.py:106-114`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/model.py#L106-L114) |

## Flow

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["window y (float array)"] --> B["prepare_target<br>no NaN"]
    B --> C["point = statistic"]
    B --> D["q10, q90 = quantile 10/90"]
    C --> E{"q10 <= point <= q90?"}
    D --> E
    E -- no --> F["q10 = min(q10, point)<br>q90 = max(q90, point)"]
    E -- yes --> G["keep"]
    F --> H["build rows"]
    G --> H
    H --> I["for h in 1..H:<br>x = future[h]<br>y = point<br>q10 = q10<br>q90 = q90"]

    classDef dark fill:#2d333b,stroke:#6d5dfc,color:#e6edf3
    class A,B,C,D,E,F,G,H,I dark
```

<!-- Sources: src/model.py:89-114 -->

## Why the clamp is necessary

The mean and the 10th/90th percentile are computed on the same window, but they
are not ordered by construction. A window with one very large spike has a mean
above its 90th percentile; a `last` value that is the minimum of the window is
below its 10th percentile. In both cases the point would lie outside its own
interval, which is incoherent for a forecast
([`src/model.py:93-97`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/model.py#L93-L97)).

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Skewed["Skewed window"]
        M["mean = 14,029"] --> Q["q90 = 39,225"]
    end
    subgraph LastMin["Last = minimum"]
        L["last = 1,090"] --> Q10["q10 = 1,469"]
    end
    Skewed --> C1["clamp q90 up to mean<br>no change needed"]
    LastMin --> C2["clamp q10 down to last"]

    classDef dark fill:#2d333b,stroke:#6d5dfc,color:#e6edf3
    class M,Q,L,Q10,C1,C2 dark
```

<!-- Sources: src/model.py:92-97 -->

The rule is minimal: only the violating bound moves, and only as far as the
point. The interval never narrows.

## Why the output is flat

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant W as window
    participant F as forecast
    participant R as rows

    W->>F: y[n-k .. n-1]
    F->>F: point = mean(W)
    F->>F: q10, q90 = quantile(W)
    loop h = 1..H
        F->>R: row(h) = {x: future[h], y: point, q10, q90}
    end
    Note over F,R: point, q10, q90 never change
```

<!-- Sources: src/model.py:99-114 -->

This is a **direct multi-step** forecast: the statistic is computed once from
observed history and never updated with its own predictions. A recursive variant
would append each forecast to the window and recompute; it is deliberately absent
([`README.md:164-172`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/README.md#L164-L172)).

### Direct vs recursive, concretely

For `k=2`, a recursive mean would produce
`f_h = y_n - (y_n - y_{n-1}) / 2^h`: the last difference is halved at every step,
so the path converges to `y_n` rather than following a trend. On AMELAG, at the
same 34-week window the recursive mean is clearly worse (MAE 13,340 vs 8,866 for
the flat mean). With a 2-week window it is marginally better than the flat
2-week mean (14,960 vs 15,222), but both are far from the 34-week flat result.
The flat model is simpler and, at the window that matters here, more accurate.

| Variant | h=1 | h=2 | h=3 | Limit | Benchmark MAE |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Flat mean k=34 | 14,029 | 14,029 | 14,029 | 14,029 | **8,866** |
| Recursive mean k=34 | 14,029 | 10,671 | 9,518 | 10,569 | 13,340 |
| Flat mean k=2 | 3,411 | 3,411 | 3,411 | 3,411 | 15,222 |
| Recursive mean k=2 | 3,411 | 3,839 | 3,625 | 4,267 | 14,960 |

Source: offline replay of the benchmark input; see the
[project README](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model#method).

## The output frame

```mermaid
erDiagram
    FORECAST_ROW {
        any x "time axis value"
        int x_auto_converted "string axis only"
        float y "repeated point"
        float y_q10 "lower bound"
        float y_q90 "upper bound"
    }
```

<!-- Sources: src/model.py:103-114, fdo.json:94-108 -->

Column names are taken from the input series, so the model is dataset-agnostic
([`src/model.py:103-104`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/model.py#L103-L104)).
If a series is unnamed, the fallbacks are `x` and `y`
([`src/model.py:103-104`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/model.py#L103-L104)).

## Validation inside `forecast`

| Check | Condition | Error |
|---|---|---|
| Horizon positive | `H > 0` | `prediction_length must be > 0` |
| Horizon bounded | `H ≤ 512` | `prediction_length=… exceeds max 512` |
| Statistic known | in `mean/median/last` | `statistic must be one of …` |
| History long enough | `len(x) ≥ 3` | `history must contain at least 3 points` |

Source: [`src/model.py:76-87`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/src/model.py#L76-L87).
These duplicate the card bounds on purpose: `forecast()` is also callable as a
library, and it should not trust its caller
([`tests/test_model.py:105-122`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/tests/test_model.py#L105-L122)).

| Page | Why read it |
|---|---|
| [Time Axis and Target Handling](https://the-episerve-consortium.github.io/model__prediction__generic__null-model/02-architecture/series-handling) | How the window array is prepared |
| [Configuration](https://the-episerve-consortium.github.io/model__prediction__generic__null-model/01-getting-started/configuration) | How `statistic` and `history_length` are chosen |

- [`tests/test_model.py`](https://github.com/The-EPISERVE-Consortium/model__prediction__generic__null-model/blob/main/tests/test_model.py)
